docs.title: SRToolkit: Symbolic Regression / Equation Discovery Benchmark Toolkit
docs.text: Documentation:: https://smeznar.github.io/SymbolicRegressionToolkit

docs.title: What is SRToolkit?
docs.text: The SRToolkit is a comprehensive Python toolkit designed to accelerate research and development in Symbolic Regression (SR) / Equation Discovery (ED). It provides a robust, easy-to-use framework for benchmarking, rapid prototyping, and mathematical expression manipulation.

docs.title: Core Features
docs.text:
SRToolkit provides a straightforward interface for:

  • Implementing new Symbolic Regression approaches and evaluating their performance against other approaches.

  • Benchmarking Symbolic Regression approaches using built-in benchmarks (currently Feynman and Nguyen) or custom data.

  • Experiment organization and postprocessing of results.

  • Converting expressions into expression trees or fast, callable NumPy functions.

  • Generating random expressions by defining the symbol space or a grammar.

  • Estimating constant parameters of expressions against real-world data.

  • Comparing and measuring the distance between expressions.

docs.title: Publications using SRToolkit
docs.text:
• T. Drnovšek. Equation discovery with Monte Carlo tree search (in Slovenian). Master's thesis, University of Ljubljana, 2026. [link] Implements the Grams approach (grammar-based Monte Carlo tree search) on SRToolkit.
  • G. Morales and A. Ekárt. Exhaustive Canonical Skeletons Generation: A Formal Dataset for Decomposable Symbolic Regression. IEEE Computational Intelligence Letters, 2026. [link] Uses SRToolkit as the infrastructure for evaluating 13 SR methods on the ExCaUS-Bench benchmark.

See the Citations page for BibTeX entries. Using SRToolkit in your work? Open an issue or a PR to have it listed.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To install the latest stable release of the package, run the following command in your terminal: 

pip install symbolic-regression-toolkit

Some built-in approaches (currently EDHiE) require extra dependencies (PyTorch and pymoo). To install them alongside the package, use the approaches extra: 

pip install 'symbolic-regression-toolkit[approaches]'

Alternatively, you can install the latest build directly from the repository with the command (Recommended):

pip install git+https://github.com/smeznar/SymbolicRegressionToolkit

docs.title: 1. Expression Manipulation (The Toolkit Core)
docs.text:
SRToolkit offers fundamental utilities for working with mathematical expressions as tokens, trees, and executable code—the building blocks for any SR approach.

import numpy as np
from SRToolkit.utils import Expression, compile_expr, tokens_to_tree, SymbolLibrary

# Create an executable function from the expression
expr = compile_expr(["X_0", "+", "X_1", "*", "C"])

# Calculate the output at two points (1, 2) and (2, 5) with C=3
data_points = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 5]])
constants = [3]
output = expr(data_points, constants)
# Variable "output" should now contain np.array([7, 17])

# Use a SymbolLibrary as a context manager to avoid passing it to every call
with SymbolLibrary.default_symbols(num_variables=2) as sl:
    # Create an expression tree from the token list
    expr_tree = tokens_to_tree(["X_0", "+", "X_1", "*", "C"])

    # Transform the expression into a list of symbols in postfix notation
    postfix_expr = expr_tree.to_list(notation="postfix")

    # Create a LaTeX string of the expression for clear presentation
    expr_latex = Expression(["X_0", "+", "X_1", "*", "C"]).to_latex()

docs.title: 2. Benchmarking and Evaluation (The Main Use Case)
docs.text:
The primary advantage of SRToolkit is its robust benchmarking framework, allowing you to quickly evaluate and compare different Symbolic Regression approaches.

from SRToolkit.approaches import EDHiE, ProGED
from SRToolkit.dataset import Feynman
from SRToolkit.evaluation import LoggingCallback
from SRToolkit.experiments import ExperimentGrid

# Load the Feynman benchmark and pick two 2-variable datasets to run on.
bm = Feynman()
ds_names = bm.list_datasets(num_variables=2, verbose=False)
dataset1 = bm.create_dataset(ds_names[0])
dataset2 = bm.create_dataset(ds_names[1])

# Define the SR approaches to benchmark.
# EDHiE requires a pre-trained/adapted model state; ProGED needs no time consuming adaptation.
edhie = EDHiE()
proged = ProGED()

# Map each (approach, dataset) pair to a file where the adapted model state will
# be saved. Both datasets reuse the same file here because they share the same
# number of variables, so one adapted state covers both.
adapted_states = {edhie.name: {ds_names[0]: "edhie_2v.pt", ds_names[1]: "edhie_2v.pt"}}

# Build the experiment grid: every combination of approach × dataset will be run
# num_experiments times (with different random seeds). Results are written under
# results_dir, specifically to "results_dir/{dataset}/{approach}/exp_{seed}.json".
eg = ExperimentGrid(
    approaches=[proged, edhie],
    datasets=[dataset1, dataset2],
    num_experiments=2,
    results_dir="results",
    adapted_states=adapted_states,
)

# Write a shell script of CLI commands that can be executed in parallel, e.g.:
#   cat commands.sh | parallel -j 4
eg.save_commands("commands.sh")

# Run adaptation for any approach/dataset pair whose adapted state file is missing.
# This is a no-op if all state files already exist.
eg.adapt_if_missing()

# Collect all pending jobs (skip any whose result file already exists on disk).
jobs = eg.create_jobs(skip_completed=True)

# Run each job sequentially in this process. To parallelize, use the generated
# commands.sh instead.
for job in jobs:
    job.run()

# See how many jobs are completed
eg.progress()

Additional examples can be found in the examples folder or in the official documentation.

docs.title: Roadmap 🗺️
docs.text:
In future releases, our primary focus will:

  • Expanded Library of Approaches: Add more Symbolic Regression approaches to the toolkit.

  • Result Visualization: Implement a robust visualization and result aggregation framework for SR results.

  • Advanced Expressions (Distant Plan): Implement support for different types of expressions, such as ODEs and PDEs.

docs.title: Contributing 🤝
docs.text:
We welcome contributions! Whether you're adding a new benchmark, implementing an SR approach, fixing a bug, or improving the documentation, please feel free to open a issue on the Github page or submit a Pull Request (PR) with a clear description of your changes.

We are especially looking for contributions of:

  • New Benchmarks and Datasets.

  • Implementations of additional Symbolic Regression Approaches (once the core framework for comparison is finalized).

Instructions on how to contribute can be found in the Contribution Guide.

docs.title: Acknowledgements
docs.text: The e-graph expression simplifier was created by Martin Perčinić and adapted for SRToolkit by Sebastian Mežnar.

docs.title: SymbolicRegressionToolkit (unreleased)
docs.text:
• The core classes are renamed to CapWords, and their modules with them: SR_approach → Approach (SRToolkit.approaches.approach), SR_dataset → Dataset (SRToolkit.dataset.dataset), SR_benchmark → Benchmark (SRToolkit.dataset.benchmark), SR_evaluator → Evaluator (SRToolkit.evaluation.evaluator), SR_results → Results and SR_callback → Callback. The parameters named after them follow: sr_evaluator → evaluator (search, run, start, ask, tell, ...) and sr_approach → approach (Dataset.evaluate_approach, adapt_or_load). The old names are removed, with no aliases. Saved benchmarks and results write "type": "Benchmark" and "type": "Results"; files saved with the old names still load.
  • Expressions (SRToolkit.utils.expression): Expression(tokens, symbol_library=None, free_constants=None) is a token list with its symbol library and the specs of its labelled constants; Expression.from_tree(node, symbol_library) builds one from a Node. It is immutable, parses its tokens once on first use and keeps the tree, whether it parses (parses, parse_error), parameter_labels, num_parameters, variables and to_latex(); resolve(default_constant) gives the full specs. It is equal to and hashed like another with the same tokens and specs, and pickles as tokens, library and specs. Public functions take list[str] | Expression; Evaluator builds one Expression per call and passes it to the constraints, the ranking and the compiler, so a new expression is parsed once (twice with simplify_expr). Stored results, checkpoints and files keep token lists and are unchanged.
  • Callbacks get a new event, on_skip(event: ExprSkipped), fired by Evaluator.count_skip (and so for every skip the step loop counts). Like the other events it may return a stop reason. TimeLimitCallback checks its limit there too, so a run that only skips (lookups, rejected samples) no longer overruns its time limit until max_consecutive_skips stops it, also in a resumed run, where the time used in earlier sessions now counts from the first skip. Callbacks are set up (saved states restored, configs recorded in EvalResult.limits) at the first counted call of evaluate_expr or count_skip; register_callbacks documents that callbacks registered later are not recorded and their saved state is not restored.
  • simplify_expr and canonicalise_constants are evaluator settings (the evaluator settings section, default False), like fold_constants: they belong to the evaluation protocol, apply to every approach, are saved with the dataset and must match on resume. They replace the parameters of evaluate_expr, get_model and get_metric, which always apply the settings, so lookups match what was scored. Candidate loses its simplify_expr and canonicalise_constants fields, and ProGED loses its canonicalise_constants option. New Evaluator.stored_tokens(expr) returns the tokens an expression is stored under; EDHiE uses it to recognise repeats within a generation as the evaluator stores them. check_constraints also runs its pre-checks on the stored form, so an empty required list again means evaluate_expr won't reject the expression in a pre-check. A malformed expression is scored "invalid" without an "Unable to simplify" warning.
  • With simplify_expr, Evaluator remembers the stored form of the 100,000 most recently used inputs, so repeats, skipped samples and lookups before an evaluation are not simplified again (a cache hit takes about a microsecond instead of tens of milliseconds), and a repeated input gets the same stored form even with simplify_max_time. The memory is not saved in checkpoints.
  • Resuming a checkpoint no longer depends on how defaults are written: a setting at its default counts as left out, so starting without method and resuming with Settings(minimize={"method": "L-BFGS-B"}) is the same run.
  • Constant folding: fold(expr, symbol_library, mode) replaces each part without a variable and with a free constant by one bare C (C*C*X_0 becomes C*X_0); the folded expression has fewer parameters but is a different hypothesis. Modes: "none", "default" (everything may fold, specs of folded labels are dropped) and "keep" (labelled constants with a spec never fold). simplify takes fold (default "none") and fold_aware (default True: pick the form that is shortest after folding, slower; False: token count, then fold). The evaluator setting fold_constants (default "none") folds every scored expression, with or without the simplify_expr setting; simplify_fold_aware sets fold_aware. The ExpressionSimplifier augmenter takes fold and fold_aware and marks folded entries with "folded": True.
  • The simplifier uses e-graphs (egglog) instead of SymPy, which is no longer a dependency. It was created by Martin Perčinić (mpercinic) and adapted by Sebastian Mežnar. simplify(expr, symbol_library, rules, max_iterations, max_nodes, max_time) returns an Expression: the simplified tokens with the specs of the labelled constants they still contain. It keeps every free constant, so the simplified expression is the same hypothesis: constant-only parts are written out (C*X_0 + C*X_0 becomes (C+C)*X_0) instead of being merged into one C. Each bare C is its own value and a label one value, so C_1 - C_1 becomes 0. The rewrite rules are a SimplificationRules object (DefaultRules(exclude=...) by default), saved like samplers; custom rules are written over EggExpr and ConstTree. Rules that rely on an operator or function the library lacks, or defines differently, are left out. Fixed values (numbers, lit symbols, fixed specs) combine into numbers when the result is finite (2*3*X_0 becomes 6*X_0). The search stops after max_iterations steps or at max_nodes e-graph entries, so results do not depend on the machine; an optional max_time (off by default) also stops it, at the cost of machine-dependent results. Simplification uses the specs an Expression carries, and the evaluator uses the new settings simplify_rules, simplify_max_iterations, simplify_max_nodes and simplify_max_time (evaluator settings section; datasets save the rules), and the ExpressionSimplifier augmenter takes rules, max_iterations, max_nodes and max_time (saved as format 2), loads its symbol library correctly, raises ValueError for an invalid scope (was a bare Exception), and handles results without models.
  • Ranking functions are now pluggable: RankingFunction with the built-in RMSERanking and BEDRanking. Evaluator and Dataset accept a built-in name ("rmse", "bed") or the import path of a custom ranking.
  • Datasets can carry a held-out test set (test_X / test_y, dataset.test) and extra data for your own measures (aux_data), stored as DataSplits. Both are saved, cached and shared with the dataset, and can be regenerated from their own data source.
  • New HoldoutMetric augmenter scores results on held-out data. It reuses the constants fitted during the search by default; refit_constants=True refits them on the held-out data instead.
  • BED:
  • takes its evaluation points from the samplers setting (the input distribution) when its behaviour comes from a ground-truth expression and num_points_sampled is not -1, otherwise from X; datasets always pass their samplers;
  • can rank expressions against the observed targets y when no ground-truth expression is given;
  • is fixed per dataset by default (ranking_seed, the dataset's seed), so every run on a dataset is scored by the same objective; ranking_resample=True resamples it per run.
  • Constant fitting is deterministic per expression: each fit's random starting point is seeded by a hash of the seed and the expression's tokens, so an expression's fit no longer depends on what was fitted before it. Under a dataset, RMSE ranking uses ranking_seed (the dataset's seed) like BED, so the same token list gets the same score in every approach and run; ranking_resample=True seeds the fits from the run's seed instead. The evaluator passes ranking_seed to the ranking's setup as its seed, so custom rankings follow it too. Fitted values differ slightly from earlier versions.
  • Added an rmse regression metric.
  • Python 3.14 support: wheels are built for 3.10–3.14, and CI tests all five versions.
  • Removed the editdistance dependency (no wheels for Python ≥ 3.13); edit_distance now uses a pure-Python Levenshtein implementation.
  • Installing from source without a C compiler now works as documented: the Cython extension is skipped and the pure-Python evaluator is used. A RuntimeWarning is issued the first time the "stack" backend falls back, and SRToolkit.utils.expression_compiler.CYTHON_AVAILABLE tells which evaluator is in use. Set SRTOOLKIT_REQUIRE_CYTHON=1 to make a failed build an error.
  • Results can be iterated over directly (for result in results:); previously such a loop ended with an AssertionError (#5).
  • Evaluator.wall_time measures a run, from the evaluator's creation until evaluation stops, and get_results always fills EvalResult.wall_time with it (previously only evaluate_approach and grid jobs set it). A resumed run's time includes its earlier sessions, and Results.from_checkpoint reads it from the checkpoint.
  • ProGED(max_consecutive_skips=...) raises a ValueError for a value below 1, which would stop the search before its first sample.
  • Results.augment(..., experiment_number=i) accepts negative numbers, as results[i] does, and raises an IndexError for an out-of-range number instead of an AssertionError.
  • SymbolLibrary(symbols, ...) and SymbolLibrary.from_symbol_list raise a ValueError for names that are not default tokens (e.g. a whole expression such as "x/(a + x)", or X_3 with num_variables=1) instead of silently dropping them (#7). The add_symbol docs show how to add a fixed composite function such as x / (1 + x) as a custom token.
  • Results record the evaluation trace: EvalResult.trace lists, for every counted evaluate_expr call, the index into all_models of the requested expression (cache hits included). New EvalResult.best_so_far(), calls_to_threshold(threshold=None) and best_error_within(budgets) compute the incumbent history, the number of calls needed to reach a threshold, and the best error within given budgets.
  • import SRToolkit no longer imports PyTorch: EDHiE and EDHiEConfig are loaded the first time they are used. This cuts the import's memory use from about 770 MB to 150 MB and makes it faster.
  • PredictFn, the type of the predict argument of the regression metrics, is exported from SRToolkit.utils.
  • create_behavior_matrix and bed take a backend argument (default "stack"), and BED ranking now respects the backend setting, which previously only applied to RMSE ranking and get_metric.
  • The docstrings of SRToolkit.utils.measures now fully specify each function: valid inputs, special values (nan, inf), exceptions, and how bed handles non-finite values.
  • Saved results and configs (ModelResult, EvalResult, ApproachConfig, HoldoutMetric) now round-trip exactly: numpy arrays keep their dtype and shape (including empty axes such as (0, 3)) and object arrays are saved element by element, tuples stay tuples, and dicts with non-string keys (int, float, tuple, numpy scalars) keep their keys. Files written by earlier versions still load. The supported values and the file format are documented on the new SRToolkit.utils.serialization reference page.
  • Expression constraints (SRToolkit.utils.expression_constraints): ExpressionConstraint checks a candidate before scoring (pre_check, on the expression) and/or after (post_check, on the fitted model), and returns a CheckResult (passed, message, amount). Built-ins: MaxConstants, MaxTokens, MaxTreeDepth, MaxTreeSize, RequiredVariables, MaxSymbolCount, NoNesting and OutputBounds. OutputBounds takes one bound for all points or one per point. A check that raises counts as failed: its CheckResult has error set, a required constraint then gives status "error", and an advisory one is recorded in advisory_violations.
  • Evaluator takes required_constraints (a failed check gives status "rejected") and advisory_constraints (failed checks are recorded in ModelResult.advisory_violations without changing the error). check_constraints(expr) runs the pre-checks without evaluating, billing or recording anything, and returns the failed required and advisory checks as two lists. max_constants / max_expr_length add a MaxConstants / MaxTokens in front of the list unless it already has one.
  • Background knowledge on datasets (SRToolkit.dataset.background_knowledge): BackgroundKnowledge holds what a task tells the approach besides the data (symbol library, samplers, constant bounds, advisory constraints, a reference grammar, task/variable/target descriptions as VariableInfo), without the answer. Dataset, from_samplers, Benchmark.add_dataset and add_from_samplers take its parts as arguments (variables=, target=, description=, advisory_constraints=, reference_grammar=, …) and expose it as dataset.background_knowledge. Its advisory constraints are stored set up on its symbol library, so their checks can run. dataset.describe() renders it for people and LLM prompts without the ground truth.
  • Dataset takes required_constraints, and max_constants / max_expr_length are named parameters that become MaxConstants / MaxTokens in that list. create_evaluator passes the required constraints and the background knowledge's advisory ones to the evaluator. constant_bounds is a named parameter too and goes into the background knowledge.
  • Samplers can be given as a mapping {token: sampler}.
  • Expression constraints describe themselves: describe() gives a short phrase (e.g. "at most 8 free constants") and summary() a plain record (e.g. {"kind": "max_constants", "limit": 8}). BackgroundKnowledge.priors() and Dataset.priors() list the records of the advisory (and required) constraints, and describe() uses the phrases. Samplers describe themselves too (UniformSampling(1, 5).describe() is "uniform on [-5, -1] ∪ [1, 5]").
  • Approaches can read the task during a run: Evaluator takes variables=, target=, description= and reference_grammar=, builds background_knowledge from them, the symbol library, the advisory constraints and the constant_bounds / samplers settings, and has describe() and priors(), equal to the dataset's for an evaluator from create_evaluator. Dataset.required_constraints are stored set up on the dataset's symbol library, so approaches can run their checks.
  • ProGED without a grammar samples from the dataset's reference_grammar when it has one (logged at INFO), else from a generic grammar. A ProGED instance reused on another dataset no longer keeps the first dataset's grammar.
  • ProGED skips samples it already evaluated or that break a required constraint, so its budget goes to new valid expressions; after max_consecutive_skips (default 10000) skips in a row it stops early. skip_evaluated=False / skip_rejected=False turn either kind of skipping off.
  • EDHiE trains its HVAE on expressions from the dataset's reference_grammar when it has one (logged at INFO), else from the symbol library, keeping only expressions that pass the required constraints (EDHiE.training_expressions returns them). Its search scores already evaluated individuals with their cached error and skips ones that break a required constraint, without using the budget, with the same skip_evaluated / skip_rejected / max_consecutive_skips settings as ProGED. A trained state can be shared only between datasets with the same symbol library, reference grammar and required constraints. training_seed makes adapt reproducible and leaves the global random states as they were. EDHiE's adaptation_scope is now "never" only for a model given through weights_path; otherwise it stays "once", so an instance reused on another dataset trains for that dataset instead of keeping the first model.
  • BackgroundKnowledge.reference_grammar must use only symbols of the symbol library, brackets and numbers (ValueError otherwise; Grammar.unknown_tokens(symbol_library) lists the offending tokens), and BackgroundKnowledge.sampling_grammar() returns the grammar approaches sample from: the reference grammar, else a generic grammar for the library.
  • Evaluator.get_model(expr) returns the result of an already evaluated expression, or None, without using the budget.
  • evaluate_approach now calls prepare() before a "once" adaptation, as the docs say and ExperimentJob.run already did. ExperimentGrid.adapt_one creates the parent directories of the state path, like the other adaptation paths.
  • Dataset.original_equation is derived when not given, from the ground truth with the variable and target names (e.g. F = m*a); only a given string is saved. Benchmark.list_datasets(verbose=True) shows it, also for datasets added with add_dataset_instance (previously None).
  • Feynman and SRSD datasets carry a name and description for every variable and the target, and a task description. SRSD equations are now derived from these names.
  • Physical units (SRToolkit.utils.units): Unit is an exact unit over base dimensions. Predefined units are module constants named by their SI symbols (u.m / u.s, u.J / u.K; the seven base units and N, J, W, Pa, Hz, C, V, Ohm, F, T). Unit({"m": 1, "s": -1}) builds one from exponents; names that are not predefined must be confirmed (Unit({"bit": 1, "s": -1}, custom_units=["bit"])), so a typo such as "meter" is an error. VariableInfo takes a unit, and BackgroundKnowledge (and Dataset, from_samplers, add_dataset, add_from_samplers, Evaluator) takes named_constants=: information, including units, about named constants ("lit" symbols). describe() shows the units.
  • Every operator and function of a SymbolLibrary has a UnitRule saying how it combines units (SAME, MULTIPLY, DIVIDE, EXPONENT, UnitRule.power(k), DIMENSIONLESS). Predefined symbols have theirs built in, and a custom symbol can be given one with add_symbol(..., unit_rule=...). Libraries saved earlier load with the built-in rules.
  • New expression constraint ConsistentUnits: an expression must be dimensionally consistent and have the target's unit. Variables and named constants have units, while free constants and numbers are dimensionless. ConsistentUnits.from_background_knowledge(dataset.background_knowledge) builds it from a dataset's units.
  • DimensionalConsistency is rewritten and now sound: every expression a grammar generates under it passes ConsistentUnits with the same units (for unambiguous grammars such as Grammar.from_symbol_library). It reads how symbols combine units from the library's UnitRules. Generation can be slow for targets that combine several dimensions (see its docs).
  • Grammar.from_symbol_library builds an unambiguous grammar: postfix functions bracket their argument (( E ) ^2) and ^ groups to the left, as the parser does. Before, emitted tokens could parse to a different expression than the one derived (e.g. (a + b)^2 emitted as a + b ^2), so ProGED's grammar probabilities applied to the wrong structure.
  • The codegen backend brackets numeric literals, so a negative number under an operator that binds tighter than unary minus gives the same value as on stack and stack_py ((-2)^2 was -4 on codegen). This affected the built-in ^2..^5 and custom templates such as "{0}**2". An expression made only of numbers now also returns one value per row of X on codegen, as on the other backends, instead of a single number.
  • ExpansionContext.siblings gives a grammar constraint the finished earlier children of the current rule.

  • Labelled free constants: C_<digits> (<constant>_<digits> for a renamed constant) is one fitted parameter however often it appears, so C_0*X_0 + C_0*X_1 has one constant; bare C is still a new parameter per occurrence. Parameters are ordered by first appearance, and Expression.parameter_labels lists them in the order of ModelResult.parameters. MaxConstants / max_constants and BED count distinct parameters, and LaTeX shows labelled constants by their label. A registered symbol (e.g. a named constant C_1) takes precedence.

  • New SRToolkit.share module: share.save(obj, path) writes a dataset, benchmark or experiment grid into one .zip with its config, its data and the custom code it uses, and share.load(path_or_url) returns the object. data="all" (default), "auto" (only data the recipient cannot reproduce) or "none" chooses the data; installed bundles that define the object's custom classes are re-packed, and other .srtk files are passed with bundles=. load copies the data into the cache, keeps each config's data_source, and installs shipped code only with install_bundles=True. Grids can ship their finished runs (results=True). Test and aux data of benchmark datasets are shipped too.

  • UrlSource reads archives written by share.save, taking only the data of the dataset's own benchmark and version.
  • Results record why a run ended: EvalResult.stop_reason is "success_threshold", "max_evaluations", the reason of a callback ("time_limit" for TimeLimitCallback, "early_stopping:max_evaluations" / "early_stopping:success_threshold" for EarlyStoppingCallback), the approach's own reason, or "returned" when the search returned by itself, so runs that end with budget left are visible. print_results shows it, and results saved earlier load with None. Approaches end a search early with Evaluator.stop(reason); ProGED and EDHiE do so when max_consecutive_skips is reached, instead of warning. Callbacks stop a run by returning a reason (a string); False still works, recorded as "callback:<ClassName>".
  • An EarlyStoppingCallback reused across experiments (e.g. one instance for a whole benchmark) takes each experiment's success_threshold / max_evaluations where it was given None, instead of keeping the first experiment's.
  • Evaluator.register_callbacks with a CallbackDispatcher no longer raises NameError or drops callbacks registered before, and no longer adds the evaluator's callbacks to the given dispatcher (in evaluate_approach, every run added another EarlyStoppingCallback to it). Breaking changes:
  • Expressions are a token list or an Expression: a Node passed to any public function (compile_expr, evaluate_expr, simplify, the measures, constraints, ground truths, …) raises a TypeError; wrap it with Expression.from_tree(node, symbol_library). A tree's leaves must be strings (Node("2.0"), not Node(2.0)), as in token lists. expr_to_latex(expr) is removed; use Expression(expr).to_latex(). simplify returns an Expression instead of a token list or Node. ExpressionConstraint.pre_check and RankingFunction.score get an Expression (read expr.tokens or expr.tree). A ground truth that cannot be used (malformed, or with specs that do not fit the default spec) now raises when Evaluator, Dataset or Benchmark.add_dataset is created, instead of when it is scored.
  • Settings are one Settings object instead of flat keyword arguments (SRToolkit.utils.settings). It has a frozen section per component, each checking its values: evaluator (simplification, folding, max_consecutive_skips, max_constants, max_expr_length, backend, ranking_seed), estimation (initialization), minimize (the optimizer's method, tol, gtol, max_iter), rmse and bed (num_points_sampled, num_consts_sampled, bed_gt); a custom ranking adds its own SettingsSection. Evaluator, Dataset, from_samplers, Benchmark.add_dataset / add_from_samplers, ParameterEstimator and HoldoutMetric take settings= and no longer accept the flat keywords; RankingSettings is removed. Evaluator(X, y, method="Nelder-Mead", simplify_expr=True) becomes Evaluator(X, y, settings=Settings(minimize={"method": "Nelder-Mead"}, evaluator={"simplify_expr": True})).
  • Facts about the task are named arguments, not settings: Evaluator takes constant_bounds, default_constant and samplers, and puts them in its background_knowledge. RankingFunction.setup(X, y, ground_truth, background_knowledge, seed, settings) gets them and the whole Settings; default_settings() is removed (defaults live in the sections). HoldoutMetric takes background_knowledge= and settings=; pass the search evaluator's.
  • ranking_resample is a dataset parameter (Dataset(..., ranking_resample=True)), not a setting. dataset.settings and dataset.ranking_resample replace dataset.kwargs, and ranking_settings() is removed. A dataset's settings may not change evaluator.max_constants / max_expr_length (ValueError); use the named parameters.
  • Datasets and benchmark entries are saved with format_version: 5 ("settings" and "ranking_resample" instead of "kwargs"). Formats 2–4 still load, with their keyword settings moved into sections; a key that is not a built-in setting (e.g. a custom ranking's) raises a ValueError: move it into a section named after the ranking.
  • Checkpoints written before this change cannot be resumed (settings are now fingerprinted as section.field).
  • Evaluator.evaluate_expr returns the expression's ModelResult (its error, fitted parameters, status and status_detail) instead of only the error, so search approaches get what tell gets; use .error for the number. After evaluation has stopped it returns None instead of nan.
  • Evaluator.should_stop is read-only (stop_reason is not None); call stop(reason) instead of setting it. The evaluator enforces success_threshold and max_evaluations itself instead of through an EarlyStoppingCallback in its callbacks. CallbackDispatcher.on_expr_evaluated / on_best_expression return the first stop reason or None instead of a bool, and EarlyStoppingCallback / TimeLimitCallback return their reason instead of False. max_evaluations=0 raises a ValueError (it used to allow one call) and a non-integer one (e.g. None) a TypeError; any negative value means no limit. register_callbacks raises a TypeError for anything but an Callback, a CallbackDispatcher or None.
  • A symbol library has exactly one free constant unless told otherwise: SymbolLibrary(...), from_symbol_list and default_symbols take const_symbol="C" and always include it (rename it with e.g. const_symbol="K", leave it out with const_symbol=None). Libraries built without listing "C", including SymbolLibrary(), now contain it. A library has at most one "const" symbol: add_symbol and SymbolLibrary.from_dict raise a ValueError for a second one. SymbolLibrary.constant_symbol gives its name. The simplifier now handles any constant name.
  • DimensionalConsistency takes (variable_units, target_unit, symbol_library, named_constant_units=None) with Unit objects; constant_units is now named_constant_units, allow_unit_polymorphic_constants is removed (free constants are dimensionless), and the tables TRANSCENDENTAL_FNS, UNIT_PRESERVING_FNS, SQRT_FNS and CBRT_FNS are removed (unit rules come from the library). Files saved by earlier versions cannot be loaded and raise a ValueError saying so.
  • Removed the RMSE, BED and R2 augmenters; use HoldoutMetric.
  • SRCallbacks is renamed Callback, in line with Approach, Dataset and the other core classes.
  • Removed the bed_X and domain_bounds settings; pass the points as X with num_points_sampled=-1, or give samplers.
  • ground_truth must be an expression (token list or Expression); a precomputed behavior matrix goes in the bed_gt setting.
  • Removed Evaluator.to_dict / from_dict; serialise the dataset instead.
  • Datasets are saved with format_version: 3; loading format_version: 1 configs is no longer supported (version 2 still loads).
  • EvalResult stores all_models (in first-seen order), trace, success_threshold and top_k; min_error, best_expr, success, num_evaluated and evaluation_calls are now read-only properties derived from them, so the constructor no longer takes them. top_models is now a method, top_models(k=None), returning the k best models (default top_k); it returns the same objects as all_models, breaks ties in error by expression length (shorter first) and then by first-seen order, and is no longer written to JSON. Results are saved with format_version: 2; results saved by earlier versions cannot be loaded and raise a ValueError saying so.
  • Evaluator.models is a list in first-seen order instead of a dict keyed by the expression string, and total_evaluations is a read-only property (len(trace)).
  • Calls to evaluate_expr after evaluation has stopped are no longer counted in total_evaluations / evaluation_calls.
  • The module-level sampling helpers in SRToolkit.dataset.sampling (uniform_sampling, log_uniform_sampling, …) are now private; use the UniformSampling, LogUniformSampling and IntegerUniformSampling classes.
  • Regression metrics (mse, rmse, mae, r2, nrmse) raise a ValueError unless predict(X) and y are 1-D of length len(X). Previously a (n, 1) target was silently broadcast against (n,) predictions into an (n, n) array, giving a meaningless value.
  • r2 and nrmse with constant targets return 1.0 / 0.0 for an exact prediction and -inf / inf otherwise, instead of nan. predict is now always called, so its exceptions propagate.
  • REGRESSION_METRICS is a read-only mapping.
  • Approach.adapt(X, symbol_library) is now adapt(X, background_knowledge, required_constraints); the symbol library is background_knowledge.symbol_library. Adapted states cached with adaptation_scope="once" were built from the old input and are reused as is; delete them (or adapt_one(..., force=True)) to re-adapt.
  • Approach.prepare is removed and no longer called; set up the search state in search (or start) instead.
  • save_adapted_state / load_adapted_state must use exactly path: the framework restores a state only if that file exists.
  • tokens_to_tree raises a TypeError for anything but a list of token strings, and compile_expr and compile_expr_rmse for anything but a token list or an Expression (previously a bare Exception, or numpy's "expected str instance" message). Numbers in token lists must be strings ("1.5"); passing 1.5 now says so.
  • Invalid arguments to edit_distance, tree_edit_distance, create_behavior_matrix and bed raise TypeError or ValueError naming the offending parameter, instead of a bare Exception, UnboundLocalError or AttributeError (a string or tuple passed to edit_distance used to be compared character by character). bed and create_behavior_matrix now validate num_consts_sampled, consts_bounds, num_points_sampled, matrix shapes and the row counts of matrices against X.
  • Values that cannot be saved as JSON (complex numbers, datetime64, sets, masked arrays, arbitrary objects) in augmentations, ranking data or approach configs now raise a TypeError from to_dict naming the value's location (for results the full path, e.g. all_models[3].ranking_data['z']), instead of failing later in json.dump. Saved arrays now include dtype and shape, and tuples and non-string-keyed dicts are written in a new form, so files saved by this version cannot be read by earlier versions.
  • ModelResult.from_dict raises a ValueError for a status that is not one of STATUSES, instead of failing later in status_counts with a KeyError.
  • The grammar base class Constraint is renamed GrammarConstraint.
  • The status_detail of a rejected expression names the constraint, e.g. "MaxConstants: 9 constants, limit 8" instead of "9 constants exceed max_constants=8".
  • max_constants / max_expr_length must be ints (numpy ints accepted); other values raise a ValueError instead of being silently ignored. Giving one together with a required constraint of the same class and a different limit raises a ValueError; a negative setting adds no limit and never clashes.
  • Saved datasets keep the symbol library and samplers inside "background_knowledge" and the limits in "required_constraints" (format 4; see format 5 above), and older files keep their data cache. Dataset.symbol_library, samplers and constant_bounds are read-only, and samplers is a tuple. A sampler count that differs from the number of variables now raises a ValueError.
  • Benchmark.add_dataset raises a ValueError (instead of Exception) when the ground truth cannot be evaluated, and a ValueError when neither dataset nor data_source is given (such an entry could never be loaded).

  • Dataset.original_equation is a read-only property.

  • Dataset.to_archive / from_archive / from_url, Benchmark.to_archive / from_archive / from_url, ExperimentGrid.export / from_export, data_cache.import_archive and data_cache.extract_zip_into_version_dir are removed; use share.save / share.load. share.load does not read the archives they wrote (a UrlSource still reads their data).

  • ExperimentGrid.save() is renamed checkpoint(), and ExperimentGrid.load(path) is removed: ExperimentGrid.from_dict(path) now also restores the adapted_states saved in the file. ExperimentGrid stores adapted_states paths as absolute paths, so a checkpoint resumes from any working directory. Fixes:
  • HoldoutMetric no longer applies the estimator's default limit of 8 constants when fitting constants on held-out data: it never applies max_constants / max_expr_length. Before, a model the search accepted (e.g. under a required MaxConstants(20)) got NaN on the holdout.
  • HoldoutMetric with a RankingFunction metric gives NaN to models the search did not score "ok", like the built-in and callable metrics already did. Before, it scored rejected models on the held-out data, so they could look like valid answers.
  • A dataset with custom constant_bounds scored every expression with a constant as NaN after a JSON round trip (from_dict, archives, ExperimentGrid).
  • Dataset.refresh() regenerates the test and aux data too, and data_cache.remove deletes them.
  • Saving results no longer fails on dict keys that are numpy scalars (e.g. np.int64) or on object arrays holding arrays.
  • Dataset now describes BED datasets correctly.
  • Compiled expressions given fewer constants than they use raise a ValueError on every backend. The default "stack" backend used to read past the end of the array and return garbage values. A SampleSource whose ground truth has a free constant (C) now fails with a clear error, as Dataset.resample already did, instead of generating a dataset with garbage y; the custom-dataset guide example that used one is fixed (#4).
  • EvalResult saves metadata like its other fields, so tuples, numpy arrays and numpy scalars in it round-trip exactly; previously a numpy value made json.dump fail and tuples came back as lists. A numpy wall_time no longer breaks saving either.
  • add_augmentation (on ModelResult and EvalResult) stores a shallow copy of data and no longer adds "_type" to the caller's dict.
  • EvalResult.calls_to_threshold ignores models with a non-finite error, like the other trace metrics.
  • Augmenters with scope="all" annotated the top models twice (e.g. ExpressionToLatex and ExpressionToLatex_1).
  • Fixed examples in the benchmarking, grammars, quickstart and experiments guides and the README (a wrong benchmark, a derivation that never finished, inconsistent file names) (#5).
  • bed gave wrong values when called with two behavior matrices that have different numbers of columns, e.g. a ground-truth matrix sampled with a different num_consts_sampled. BEDRanking always compares matrices of equal width, so rankings were not affected.
  • bed returned 0 for points where one expression is nan and the other infinite, or where they are +inf and -inf. Such points now give inf; points where both expressions are the same infinity give 0, as documented.
  • Evaluating an expression on an X with too few columns (or a 1-D X) read past the end of the array on the default "stack" backend and returned garbage; it now raises a ValueError. This affected compile_expr, create_behavior_matrix and bed.
  • tree_edit_distance priced relabelling by the character edit distance between symbols when the optional editdistance package was installed, so results depended on the environment. It now always uses unit costs.
  • Regression metrics no longer emit NumPy warnings on empty or non-finite input; the returned nan / inf is the signal.
  • MaxOccurrences let a grammar rule containing the symbol several times (e.g. E -> x * x) exceed the limit.
  • Benchmark.create_dataset no longer turns every error from loading an entry into a bare ValueError: TypeError, ImportError and FileNotFoundError pass through, and a ValueError keeps its cause.
  • Dataset and Benchmark.add_dataset raise a ValueError when the data's number of columns differs from the number of variables in the symbol library. Such a dataset was accepted before and failed or misbehaved later (e.g. list_datasets(num_variables=...) missed it, resampling drew the wrong number of columns).
  • Benchmark.from_dict no longer modifies the dict it is given.
  • Dataset.evaluate_approach seeds experiment i with initial_seed + i (or the dataset seed + i), like ExperimentGrid does. It used + i + 1, so the given seed itself was never used; runs with the same initial_seed now give different results than before (use initial_seed + 1 to reproduce them).
  • is_float returns False for values float cannot convert (lists, complex numbers, arbitrary objects) instead of raising a TypeError.
  • An Evaluator whose required constraints allow more than 8 free constants no longer has its parameter estimator reject such expressions at its default limit of 8.
  • SRSD Bonus 6: the ground truth used epsilon instead of epsilon**2. Fixed together with its data (SRSD data version 1.0.1); its targets no longer contain NaN.
  • UrlSource on a dataset's test or aux data extracted the archive into that split's folder instead of the dataset's version folder.
  • Free constants can be specified per constant (SRToolkit.utils.free_constants). Write a constant labelled (C_0, …) to make every occurrence one parameter, and give it a Constant spec: a prior, fitting bounds (infinite ends allowed), a starting value, or a fixed value. An Expression carries the specs of its constants, and Evaluator.evaluate_expr, RankingFunction.score, ParameterEstimator, create_behavior_matrix and bed use them, and results record them (ModelResult.free_constants, EvalResult.default_constant; results format 3, format 2 still loads). Constants without a spec use the dataset's default spec (BackgroundKnowledge.default_constant, by default uniform on constant_bounds). A ground truth given as an Expression carries its specs (dataset.ground_truth_constants shows them), so a ground truth with fixed constants (e.g. 9.81) can generate y, and BED samples the ground truth's constants from its specs. Bare-C expressions keep their scores. The evaluator's cache no longer merges different token lists that join to the same string. BED's default success threshold is at least 1e-7.
  • ParameterEstimator no longer has the max_constants / max_expr_length settings: it fits every expression it is given. Evaluator enforces both limits as required constraints (MaxConstants, MaxTokens), as before, and HoldoutMetric no longer applies them to refits.
  • New canonicalise writes the free constants of an expression one way: a constant that occurs once is bare C, a shared one C_<k> by its position, so C_0*X_0 + C_0 and C_1*X_0 + C_1 become the same tokens; it returns an Expression. The evaluator setting canonicalise_constants applies it, for approaches that write labelled constants. Grammars can generate shared constants with C_0, C_1, … terminals; EDHiE trains on them as bare C.
  • SymbolLibrary stores each token as an immutable Symbol record. get(token) (returns None for brackets, numbers and unknown tokens) and sl[token] (raises KeyError) replace get_type, get_precedence, get_np_fn, get_cython_id, get_latex_str and get_unit_rule. add_symbol's np_fn argument is renamed python_str (it is a Python expression template, not only NumPy); saved files keep the np_fn key. preamble is replaced by modules (alias → module path, e.g. {"sp": "scipy.special"}), which custom symbols can use on every backend; modules imported through preamble other than NumPy never worked (NameError). Saved libraries still load; a saved preamble may contain only import numpy as np.
  • Loading a saved sampler, data source, approach, callback or grammar constraint checks that the class named in it is of that kind and raises a TypeError otherwise (before, that class's from_dict was called). build_ranking raises TypeError instead of ValueError for an import path that is not a RankingFunction. A saved dict that names the base class itself (e.g. Sampler) raises a TypeError instead of recursing forever; for ExpressionConstraint this was a NotImplementedError.
  • New Dataset.adapt_or_load(approach, path, force=False): adapts an approach to a dataset, or loads its saved adapted state from path. evaluate_approach, grid jobs and ExperimentGrid.adapt_one all use it.
  • Evaluator keeps its models and trace in SQLite: in memory by default, or in a file with checkpoint=path, which keeps memory constant during long runs (committed every 1000 new models or 30 s, when evaluation stops and when results are collected). se.models and se.trace are now read-only, live views instead of lists, and se.models[i] returns a new ModelResult on each access. A model whose ranking output cannot be saved gets status "error" instead of failing later when the results are saved. ModelResult and samplers compare by value (to_dict), so models with fitted parameters can be compared and samplers loaded from a file equal the originals.
  • Checkpoints: Evaluator(..., checkpoint=path) writes its models and trace to a SQLite file as it goes, and Results.from_checkpoint(path) turns one into results, also while the run is going or after a crash. Approaches can implement an optional step interface: start returns a search state, which ask and tell receive and change in place, so a run never changes the approach object and nothing carries over to the next run; dump_search_state / load_search_state serialise it for snapshots (pickle by default). ask proposes token lists, Nodes or Candidates (with free-constant specs, or a skip reason to only look up an expression, spending no budget), and tell gets them back with their ModelResults (None for a skip that was never evaluated); the framework runs the loop and snapshots the approach's state between steps, and Evaluator(..., resume=True) with Approach.run continues a run from its last snapshot. ProGED implements it. A resume refuses a checkpoint whose data, ranking, constraints, symbol library, default constant, seed or limits differ. Callbacks can save runtime state (get_state / set_state); TimeLimitCallback counts time across sessions and ProgressBarCallback shows the call count.
  • Runs can be interrupted and resumed: Dataset.evaluate_approach(..., checkpoint_dir=..., resume=..., keep_checkpoint=...) and ExperimentJob checkpoint each experiment ({dataset}/{approach}/exp_{seed}.sqlite). The first Ctrl-C or SIGTERM stops the search at the end of the current step and keeps the checkpoint, so a SLURM job stopped before its time limit loses no work; a second one aborts. Running again (with resume=True for evaluate_approach) continues where it stopped. An interrupted job saves no result and the run_job CLI exits with status 130. Checkpoints are deleted once the results are saved, unless keep_checkpoint keeps them compacted. Evaluator.stop_on_signals() and Evaluator.step() provide the signal handling for custom loops. Results.save now writes files atomically.
  • Results of long runs: keep_all_models=False (on get_results, Results.from_checkpoint, evaluate_approach, ExperimentInfo and ExperimentGrid) keeps only the top_k models and a RunSummary (counts, the best-so-far history with its models, status counts, the Pareto front), so memory and result files no longer grow with the run; the methods of EvalResult give the same answers. New EvalResult.pareto_front(). A result whose checkpoint was kept refers to it (EvalResult.checkpoint), and open_checkpoint() opens it read-only to reach all models; ExperimentGrid(keep_checkpoint=True) keeps the checkpoints of a grid's jobs. Keeping more than 1,000,000 models warns. Results are saved in format 4; earlier files still load.
  • Job status for grids: a running ExperimentJob holds a lock (exp_{seed}.lock, fcntl.flock), so the same job never runs in two processes at once (a second run() raises RuntimeError; without file locking, e.g. on Windows, it warns and runs unlocked). ExperimentJob.status reads a job's state from its files: done, running, not started, interrupted or crashed. ExperimentGrid.progress() (and the progress CLI) also lists running, interrupted and crashed jobs; create_jobs and save_commands skip running jobs as well as done ones. ExperimentGrid(snapshot_interval=...) sets the snapshot interval of its jobs.
  • ExperimentJob.run() on a done job does nothing; run(rerun=True) (CLI run_job --rerun) deletes its result and checkpoint and runs it afresh. commands --all / save_commands(skip_completed=False) add --rerun to the lines of done jobs.
  • EDHiE implements the step interface (one generation of its genetic algorithm per step), so its runs resume from snapshots; resuming needs the same HVAE and settings, and a different HVAE raises a ValueError. Seeded EDHiE runs are now reproducible (pymoo's own random generator was unseeded), and individuals that were already evaluated or break a required constraint are proposed as lookups, which use no budget. In the step interface, ask may return None for a proposal that is not an expression; tell gets None for it. EDHiE.save_adapted_state raises a RuntimeError when there is no HVAE to save, instead of warning and writing nothing.
  • ProGED makes one derivation attempt per step: a failed derivation (more than 1000 rule applications, or no rule fits) is proposed as None and counted as the skip "not_expression", instead of being redrawn. Samples are no longer silently limited to 50 tokens (a MaxTokens constraint rejects long ones), and a grammar that never yields an expression ends the run through max_consecutive_skips instead of raising an Exception. ProGED.start(seed=None) leaves NumPy's global random state as it is instead of reseeding it from fresh entropy.
  • Runs can be extended with new limits: Dataset.extend_run(approach, checkpoint, max_evaluations=..., success_threshold=..., callbacks=...) continues a run, finished or interrupted, from its last snapshot (a larger budget, a lower threshold, a longer time limit); ExperimentJob.extend(...) does the same for a grid job and saves its result. A step cut short by a stop is no longer snapshotted, so an extended run equals one that had the new limits from the start (for approaches deterministic from their state). An extension that changes nothing is a plain resume. A plain resume with changed limits still raises, now pointing to extend_run; one that meets a limit at once stops without a call.
  • Results count what an approach skipped without evaluating it: Evaluator.count_skip(reason) (no budget) adds to Evaluator.skips, saved as EvalResult.skips (e.g. {"evaluated": 12, "rejected": 3}) and in checkpoints; a resumed run continues from the counts of its snapshot. In the step interface a candidate with a reason (Candidate(expr, skip="rejected")) is looked up instead of evaluated, and the step loop counts it, and a None entry as "not_expression", when it reaches it. The new evaluator setting max_consecutive_skips (default 10000, negative for no limit) stops a run after that many skips in a row with the reason "max_consecutive_skips"; every counted evaluate_expr call resets the count. It replaces the skip limits of ProGED and EDHiE: ProGED's max_consecutive_skips option is removed, EDHiE's is renamed max_training_skips (old configs still load) and only limits sampling its training expressions, and neither stops with its own reason any more. ProGED now proposes each skipped sample as a lookup, one sample per step, as EDHiE does, instead of sampling until it finds one to evaluate. Evaluator.close() also saves the wall time and skip counts, so a checkpoint closed during a run keeps them. Evaluations are not counted again: calls that repeat an evaluated model are evaluation_calls - num_evaluated, rejected calls status_counts(per="call")["rejected"].
  • Results record their limits: EvalResult.limits holds one segment for the start of a run and one per extension (budget, threshold, the callbacks' configs and the previous stop reason), and EvalResult.extended says whether a run was extended. A resume with other callbacks than those recorded warns, as does a saved callback state whose callback moved to another position.

docs.title: SymbolicRegressionToolkit-1.6.0 (2026-06-23)
docs.text:
• New backends for expression evaluations (about 1.5x speedup for parameter estimation)
  • SymbolLibrary can now be as a global default or used with the ContextManager (with SymbolLibrary()...:)
  • Added grammars (CFG, PCFG) and the ability to add constraints to them.
  • Added a TimeLimitCallback
  • Added wallclock time to experiment
  • Added some default constraints that work as built-ins and reference implementations
  • Added guides to the documentation
  • Added some tests
  • Reworked how sharing code/benchmark works:
  • Code is shared through bundles, which can be installed and are directly usable after
  • Datasets/benchmarks are versioned and can be shared via .zip files, of through configs implementing DataSources
  • Configs should be shared directly and should be run through pack, so they are directly usable
  • ExperimentGrid can now be exported together with all the bundles and data it needs. Custom code is shipped only via re-packed installed bundles or explicit .srtk files passed to export(additional_bundles=...) (no more guessing a bundle from a loose source file); uncovered classes warn, or raise with export(strict=True)

docs.title: SymbolicRegressionToolkit-1.5.0 (2026-04-14)
docs.text:
• Reworked how SR_results and ResultAugmenters work
  • Improved documentation
  • Fixed some bugs
  • Made the interface more consistent and easier to use
  • Two instances of SR_benchmarks are now in separate files and allow resampling of data
  • All (or at least all relevant) classes can now be saved and loaded/transformed into and from a dictionary
  • Added some tests (a lot more to go)
  • Added new examples

New Features:

  • Added a base class for approaches and implemented ProGED and EDHiE
  • Added a way to run generate and run experiments easily
  • Added the callback system to allow custom events during experiments

docs.title: SymbolicRegressionToolkit-1.4.0 (2025-10-28)
docs.text:
• Updated documentation
  • Rewrote the SR_dataset and SR_benchmark classes
  • New readme and logo

New Features:

  • Added ResultAugmenter to augment result of evaluation with additional measures, simplification of best expressions, etc.
  • Added distance measures
  • Added BED as a possible ranking measure for evaluation

docs.title: SymbolicRegressionToolkit-1.3.2 (2025-07-07)
docs.text:
• Updated documentation

New Feature:

  • Added a way to generate expressions
  • Expression simplification now more or less works

Bug Fixes:

  • Feynman dataset and Nguyen datasets are now almost done
  • Small fixes to different functionalities

docs.title: SymbolicRegressionToolkit-1.2.6 (2025-04-26)
docs.text:
• Updated documentation
  • Added the change log

New Features:

  • Expressions can now be transformed into latex code
  • Added Dataset and benchmark objects that create evaluators for Symbolic Regression models
  • Added modified versions of feynman and nguyen benchmarks

Bug Fixes:

  • Fixed expressions with constants only evaluating to one value instead of an array

docs.title: SymbolicRegressionToolkit-1.1.0 (2024-12-10)
docs.text:
• Project restructure

New Features:

  • Added documentation
  • Expanded upon examples

docs.title: SymbolicRegressionToolkit-1.0.0 (2024-12-06)
docs.text:
• Initial release
  • Expression compilation
  • Parameter estimation
  • Model evaluation
  • Examples for parameter estimation and performance evaluation

docs.title: Citations
docs.text: This page lists how to cite SRToolkit and the publications behind the benchmarks and approaches included in the toolkit. Click any entry to expand it and copy the BibTeX.

docs.title: Citing SRToolkit
docs.text:
If you use SRToolkit in your research, please cite:

Mežnar et al. (2026) — SRToolkit: Shared Infrastructure for Symbolic Regression Research

Mežnar, S., Todorovski, L. & Džeroski, S. (2026). IEEE WCCI 2026 Workshop on Symbolic Regression (SymReg 2026), oral presentation. https://openreview.net/forum?id=du21XftP2Q

@inproceedings{Meznar2026SRToolkit,
  title     = {{SRToolkit: Shared Infrastructure for Symbolic Regression Research}},
  author    = {Me{\v{z}}nar, Sebastian and Todorovski, Ljup{\v{c}}o
               and D{\v{z}}eroski, Sa{\v{s}}o},
  booktitle = {IEEE WCCI 2026 Workshop on Symbolic Regression (SymReg 2026)},
  year      = {2026},
  url       = {https://openreview.net/forum?id=du21XftP2Q}
}

To cite a specific version of the software, use:

Mežnar (2026) — SRToolkit, version 1.6.0

Mežnar, S. (2026). SRToolkit: Symbolic Regression / Equation Discovery Benchmark Toolkit, version 1.6.0. https://github.com/smeznar/SymbolicRegressionToolkit

@software{Meznar2026SRToolkitSoftware,
  title   = {{SRToolkit: Symbolic Regression / Equation Discovery Benchmark Toolkit}},
  author  = {Me{\v{z}}nar, Sebastian},
  year    = {2026},
  version = {1.6.0},
  url     = {https://github.com/smeznar/SymbolicRegressionToolkit}
}

docs.text:
Drnovšek (2026) — Equation discovery with Monte Carlo tree search

Drnovšek, T. (2026). Odkrivanje enačb z drevesnim preiskovanjem Monte Carlo [Equation discovery with Monte Carlo tree search]. Master's thesis, University of Ljubljana, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics. In Slovenian. Implements the Grams approach (grammar-based Monte Carlo tree search) on SRToolkit. http://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12556/RUL-187297

Morales, G. & Ekárt, A. (2026). IEEE Computational Intelligence Letters, 1–6. Uses SRToolkit as the infrastructure for evaluating 13 SR methods on the ExCaUS-Bench benchmark. https://doi.org/10.1109/LCI.2026.3753204

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Step-by-step guides for common tasks in SRToolkit.

Guide Description Quickstart Install the toolkit and run your first benchmark Expression Manipulation Work with expressions as tokens, trees, and functions Benchmarking SR Approaches Evaluate and compare approaches on built-in benchmarks Running Experiments Organise multi-run experiments and collect results Implementing a Custom Approach Wrap your own SR algorithm for use with SRToolkit Creating a Custom Dataset Define and register your own datasets and benchmarks Grammar-Guided Generation Control expression structure with CFG/PCFG grammars and constraints Sharing Custom Implementations Package and share custom approaches, constraints, samplers, and experiment bundles

docs.title: Loading a benchmark
docs.text:
SRToolkit ships with three benchmark collections. Data is downloaded or generated automatically on first use.

from SRToolkit.dataset import Feynman, Nguyen, SRSD_Feynman

bm = Feynman()       # 100 physics equations, downloads ~10 MB on first use
bm = Nguyen()        # 10 polynomial / trig expressions
bm = SRSD_Feynman()  # 120 physics equations with per-variable sampling

docs.title: Listing and creating datasets
docs.text:
# Print a summary table of all datasets
bm.list_datasets()

# Filter by number of variables
names = bm.list_datasets(num_variables=2, verbose=False)

# Create a Dataset ready for evaluation
dataset = bm.create_dataset(names[0])

print(dataset.X.shape)          # (n_samples, n_variables)
print(dataset.y.shape)          # (n_samples,)
print(dataset.original_equation)

docs.title: Evaluating an approach
docs.text:
Pass any Approach to dataset.evaluate_approach():

from SRToolkit.approaches import ProGED

model = ProGED()

# Run 5 independent experiments and keep the top 20 expressions each
results = dataset.evaluate_approach(model, num_experiments=5, top_k=20, initial_seed=0)

results is an Results object. Inspect individual runs:

for r in results:
    print(r.dataset_name, r.approach_name, r.best_expr, r.min_error, r.success)

docs.title: Resampling data
docs.text:
Pass n_samples (and optionally seed) to create_dataset() to draw a fresh sample using the same distribution as the original data:

bm = Feynman()

ds = bm.create_dataset("I.16.6", n_samples=500, seed=42)
X, y = ds.X, ds.y

The cache is not modified — only the returned Dataset instance contains the new data.

For SRSD_Feynman, this uses the per-variable sampling objects (log-uniform, linear, integer) defined for each equation.

docs.title: Using callbacks
docs.text:
Callbacks attach to the evaluator and fire events during search. Pass them to evaluate_approach():

from SRToolkit.evaluation.callbacks import (
    EarlyStoppingCallback,
    LoggingCallback,
    ProgressBarCallback,
)

results = dataset.evaluate_approach(
    model,
    num_experiments=5,
    callbacks=[
        ProgressBarCallback(),
        EarlyStoppingCallback(threshold=1e-6),
        LoggingCallback(log_file="logs/{dataset_name}_{seed}.log"),
    ],
)
Callback Behaviour ProgressBarCallback tqdm progress bar updated after each evaluation EarlyStoppingCallback(threshold) stops the search once error drops below threshold (the evaluator already stops at the dataset's success_threshold) LoggingCallback(log_file) appends each new best expression to a file or stdout

docs.title: Writing a custom callback
docs.text:
Subclass Callback and override only the events you need. Return a reason (a string) from on_expr_evaluated, on_best_expression or on_skip (fired for each expression the approach skips without evaluating) to stop the search early; it is saved in the results as stop_reason.

from SRToolkit.evaluation.callbacks import Callback, BestExpressionFound

class PrintEveryImprovement(Callback):
    def on_best_expression(self, event: BestExpressionFound):
        print(f"  [{event.evaluation_number}] {event.expression}  error={event.error:.4g}")

docs.title: Implementing a Custom Approach
docs.text: All SR approaches subclass Approach and implement search(), or the step interface start(), ask() and tell() (see the module docs). Optionally, override adapt() when your approach benefits from a pre-training or warm-up phase.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SRToolkit.approaches.approach import Approach, ApproachConfig
from SRToolkit.evaluation import Evaluator
from SRToolkit.utils import SymbolLibrary, generate_n_expressions
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class RandomSearchConfig(ApproachConfig):
    name: str = "RandomSearch"
    batch_size: int = 50

class RandomSearch(Approach):
    def __init__(self, batch_size: int = 50):
        super().__init__(RandomSearchConfig(batch_size=batch_size))
        self.batch_size = batch_size

    def search(self, evaluator: Evaluator, seed: int | None = None):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        sl = evaluator.symbol_library

        while not evaluator.should_stop:
            exprs = generate_n_expressions(sl, self.batch_size, verbose=False)
            for expr in exprs:
                evaluator.evaluate_expr(expr)
                if evaluator.should_stop:
                    return

docs.title: Key rules for search()
docs.text:
• Call evaluator.evaluate_expr(expr) for every candidate expression. The evaluator handles parameter fitting, caching, and result bookkeeping.
  • Check evaluator.should_stop regularly and finish search when it is True.
  • To end the search early (e.g. the search space is exhausted), call evaluator.stop("reason"); the reason is saved in the results as stop_reason.
  • Do not access target values directly — use the evaluator as the sole interface to y.

docs.title: The adapt() lifecycle
docs.text:
adapt() is called before search() and receives X (no y), the dataset's background knowledge and its required constraints (set up, so their checks can run). Use what you need for warm-up that does not require knowing the target:

def adapt(self, X, background_knowledge, required_constraints):
    # Train a generative model, build a PCFG, pre-compute statistics, etc.
    self._grammar = build_grammar(background_knowledge.symbol_library)

Control when adaptation happens via the adaptation_scope property:

Value When adapt() is called "never" (default) Never — skip adapt() entirely "once" Once per run; with a state path the state is saved and reloaded for later runs "experiment" Before every search() call

For "once" scope, also implement save_adapted_state() and load_adapted_state():

import torch

@property
def adaptation_scope(self):
    return "once"

def save_adapted_state(self, path: str):
    torch.save(self._model.state_dict(), path)

def load_adapted_state(self, path: str):
    self._model.load_state_dict(torch.load(path))

Heavy dependencies

If your approach needs heavy libraries (e.g. PyTorch, like the built-in EDHiE), do not make them hard dependencies of the toolkit. Declare them in an optional extra and guard the import so users without the extra get a clear message instead of an opaque ImportError:

try:
    import torch
except ImportError:
    raise ImportError(
        "MyApproach requires PyTorch. Install it manually or with "
        "pip install 'symbolic-regression-toolkit[approaches]'"
    )

docs.title: Configuration with ApproachConfig
docs.text:
Subclass ApproachConfig to make your approach serialisable. This enables saving/loading grids and running jobs from the command line:

@dataclass
class RandomSearchConfig(ApproachConfig):
    name: str = "RandomSearch"
    batch_size: int = 50

The config is serialised automatically when the grid is saved. To support CLI execution, your Approach subclass should also implement from_config:

@classmethod
def from_config(cls, config: dict) -> "RandomSearch":
    return cls(batch_size=config.get("batch_size", 50))

docs.title: Using the approach
docs.text:
Once implemented, the approach integrates directly with the rest of the toolkit:

from SRToolkit.dataset import Nguyen

bm = Nguyen()
dataset = bm.create_dataset("NG-1")
model = RandomSearch(batch_size=100)
results = dataset.evaluate_approach(model, num_experiments=3)

docs.title: Defining a SymbolLibrary
docs.text:
The SymbolLibrary defines which tokens an approach may use. Start from the curated default set and restrict it to what's relevant for your problem:

from SRToolkit.utils import SymbolLibrary

# Restrict to a specific token set for a 2-variable problem
sl = SymbolLibrary.from_symbol_list(
    ["+", "-", "*", "/", "sin", "cos", "exp", "sqrt", "^2", "^3", "C"],
    num_variables=2,
)

Full list of supported default tokens is documented in SymbolLibrary.default_symbols.

docs.title: Creating a standalone Dataset
docs.text:
Dataset wraps input data and evaluation settings for one problem:

import numpy as np
from SRToolkit.dataset import Dataset
from SRToolkit.utils import SymbolLibrary

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0.5, 5.0, size=(1000, 2))
y = X[:, 0] ** 2 + np.sin(X[:, 1])

sl = SymbolLibrary.from_symbol_list(
    ["+", "*", "sin", "^2", "C"], num_variables=2
)

dataset = Dataset(
    X=X,
    y=y,
    symbol_library=sl,
    dataset_name="my_equation",
    original_equation="x0^2 + sin(x1)",
    ground_truth=["X_0", "^2", "+", "sin", "(", "X_1", ")"],
    max_evaluations=50000,
    success_threshold=1e-6,
    constant_bounds=(-10.0, 10.0),
    max_expr_length=20,
)

Key parameters:

Parameter Purpose ground_truth Token list of the known solution; used to compute BED and check success success_threshold Error below which an expression counts as solved constant_bounds Search range for free constants during parameter fitting max_evaluations Budget passed to the SR approach max_expr_length Maximum token list length the evaluator will accept

docs.title: Creating a dataset from an expression and samplers
docs.text:
A very common case is having only the target expression and a sampling spec for its inputs — no data arrays yet. Dataset.from_samplers covers it in one call: it draws X from the samplers (one per variable), evaluates the ground truth to produce y, and records a SampleSource so the data can be regenerated or resampled later.

from SRToolkit.dataset import Dataset
from SRToolkit.dataset.sampling import UniformSampling

dataset = Dataset.from_samplers(
    ground_truth=["X_0", "^2", "+", "sin", "(", "X_1", ")"],
    samplers=[UniformSampling(0.5, 5.0), UniformSampling(0.5, 5.0)],
    n_samples=1000,
    seed=42,
)
print(dataset.X.shape)   # (1000, 2)

symbol_library defaults to one variable per sampler and original_equation, when not given, is derived from the ground truth with the variable and target names (y = X_0+X_1 without them), so the minimal call is just the expression and the samplers. Use ranking_function="bed" for a dataset that only needs inputs (no y). from_samplers takes the constructor's other arguments (max_evaluations, constant_bounds, settings=, …) and generates the data instead of taking X, y and the test and aux arrays.

docs.title: Building a benchmark with Benchmark
docs.text:
Group multiple datasets into a reusable benchmark by subclassing Benchmark. Provide a data_source for each dataset so data is generated (or downloaded) automatically on first use and cached locally for subsequent runs.

from SRToolkit.dataset import Benchmark
from SRToolkit.dataset.data_source import SampleSource
from SRToolkit.dataset.sampling import UniformSampling
from SRToolkit.utils import SymbolLibrary

_SYMBOL_LIST = ["+", "-", "*", "/", "sin", "cos", "^2", "^3", "C"]


class MyBenchmark(Benchmark):
    __data_version__ = "1.0.0"

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("my_benchmark", version="1.0.0")
        self._populate()

    def _populate(self):
        sl_1v = SymbolLibrary.from_symbol_list(_SYMBOL_LIST, num_variables=1)
        sl_2v = SymbolLibrary.from_symbol_list(_SYMBOL_LIST, num_variables=2)

        self.add_dataset(sl_1v, None, dataset_name="eq1", ranking_function="rmse", max_evaluations=50000,
                         ground_truth=["X_0", "^2", "+", "1"], original_equation="x^2 + 1", success_threshold=1e-6,
                         seed=42, samplers=[UniformSampling(0.5, 5.0)],
                         data_source=SampleSource(n_samples=10000, seed=42))
        self.add_dataset(sl_2v, None, dataset_name="eq2", ranking_function="rmse", max_evaluations=50000,
                         ground_truth=["sin", "(", "X_0", ")", "+", "X_1", "^2"], original_equation="sin(x0) + x1^2",
                         success_threshold=1e-6, seed=42,
                         samplers=[UniformSampling(0.5, 5.0), UniformSampling(0.5, 5.0)],
                         data_source=SampleSource(n_samples=10000, seed=42))

docs.title: Shortcut: add_from_samplers
docs.text:
When every dataset is "expression + samplers", add_from_samplers is a shorthand for the add_dataset(None, …, data_source=SampleSource(...)) form above: it wires up the SampleSource for you and defaults the symbol library to one variable per sampler. Data is still generated lazily on the first create_dataset().

self.add_from_samplers(
    ground_truth=["X_0", "^2", "+", "1"],
    samplers=[UniformSampling(0.5, 5.0)],
    dataset_name="eq1",
    n_samples=10000,
    seed=42,
    success_threshold=1e-6,
)

docs.title: The data_source field
docs.text:
data_source is a DataSource that tells the cache layer where the raw arrays come from. It describes the data's origin only — the problem's input distribution lives in samplers, which stays available for resample regardless of the source.

Source Example Behaviour SampleSource SampleSource(n_samples=N, seed=S) Generate from the dataset's samplers + ground_truth on first use; reproducible UrlSource UrlSource("https://...") Download a zip archive on first use; all datasets in the archive extracted at once None None Data was supplied directly (e.g. as arrays) and already lives in the cache; raises FileNotFoundError if absent

Need a source of your own (a simulation, a database query, a custom loader)? Subclass DataSource and implement to_dict / from_dict / materialize; it round-trips without any registration.

Data is generated or downloaded once and stored under <user_data_dir>/SRToolkit/data/<benchmark>/<version>/ (dots and hyphens in the version become underscores, e.g. 1.0.0 → 1_0_0). All subsequent calls to create_dataset() load from this cache instantly.

docs.title: Resampling
docs.text:
To get a fresh draw with a different size or seed, pass n_samples (and optionally seed) to create_dataset(). The returned dataset contains newly-sampled data; the cache is not modified.

bm = MyBenchmark()

# Standard load (from cache)
ds = bm.create_dataset("eq1")

# Fresh 500-sample draw
ds_small = bm.create_dataset("eq1", n_samples=500, seed=7)
print(ds_small.X.shape)   # (500, 1)

docs.title: Serialising a custom benchmark
docs.text:
Set benchmark and version on the benchmark (already done via super().__init__) and call to_dict() to get a portable JSON config with no filesystem side effects:

bm = MyBenchmark()
config = bm.to_dict()   # pure dict — no .npz written

import json
with open("my_benchmark.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(config, f, indent=2)

Reconstruct from the config file (data materialises on first create_dataset):

from SRToolkit.dataset import Benchmark

bm2 = Benchmark.from_dict("my_benchmark.json")
ds = bm2.create_dataset("eq1")

For self-contained sharing (data embedded in a single file), use share.save instead — see the Sharing guide.

docs.title: Loading a dataset someone shared
docs.text:
To consume a dataset or benchmark built elsewhere, pick the loader that matches how it was shared:

Shared as Load with A .zip archive, local or hosted share.load(path_or_url) (from SRToolkit import share) A JSON config / recipe Dataset.from_dict(path_or_dict) / Benchmark.from_dict(...)

The trade-offs between these channels — shipping data versus shipping a recipe that regenerates by sampling — are covered in the Sharing guide.

docs.title: Running Experiments
docs.text: ExperimentGrid manages the cross-product of datasets × approaches × seeds. Jobs can run locally or be dispatched to an HPC cluster, and results are automatically resumed if a run is interrupted.

docs.title: Setting up an ExperimentGrid
docs.text:
from SRToolkit.dataset import Feynman
from SRToolkit.approaches import EDHiE, ProGED
from SRToolkit.experiments import ExperimentGrid

bm = Feynman()
datasets = [bm.create_dataset(n) for n in bm.list_datasets(num_variables=2, verbose=False)[:4]]

# EDHiE's training depends on the symbol library, reference grammar and required constraints;
# these datasets share all three, so map each to a shared weights file
adapted_states = {
    "EDHiE": {ds.dataset_name: "edhie_2v.pt" for ds in datasets}
}

grid = ExperimentGrid(
    datasets=datasets,
    approaches=[ProGED(), EDHiE()],
    num_experiments=5,
    results_dir="results/feynman_run",
    initial_seed=0,
    adapted_states=adapted_states,
)

Results land at results_dir/{dataset}/{approach}/exp_{seed}.json. Re-running never overwrites completed jobs.

docs.title: Adapting models
docs.text:
For approaches with adaptation_scope="once" (like EDHiE), the state must be adapted once per (approach, dataset) pair before the experiments run. For a local run, call adapt_if_missing() — it adapts every pair whose state file is absent and saves it to the path given in adapted_states:

grid.adapt_if_missing()

When several datasets share one state_path (as in the EDHiE example above, where adaptation is per symbol space rather than per dataset), that path is adapted once — on the first dataset listed for it — and the remaining datasets reuse the result. An informational warning lists the shared paths so an accidental collision is easy to spot; if adaptation should differ per dataset, give each dataset a distinct state_path.

For a cluster run you don't need this: save_commands emits one parallel-safe adapt command per pair into a separate prepare file (see below).

docs.title: Running jobs locally
docs.text:
for job in grid.create_jobs():   # skips already-completed jobs by default
    job.run()

docs.title: Generating commands for parallel execution
docs.text:
For larger experiments, write a commands file and run it with GNU Parallel or a SLURM array:

grid.save_commands("results/feynman_run/commands.sh")

save_commands writes the grid to results_dir/grid.json and materialises every dataset's data into the cache once, in this process — so data is fetched a single time on the machine writing the commands (typically the only node with network access on a cluster), and the parallel workers only read it.
